appraisal_events.evidence: « J'avais appris que Gilberte était malheureuse, trompée par Robert, mais pas de la manière que tout le monde croyait » ; Jupien reveals that the letters signed Bobette come from « le violoniste qui avait joué un si grand rôle dans la vie de M. de Charlus » ; « cet excellent mari, cet amant jadis passionné de Rachel, avait dans sa vie un autre plan » ; « il était devenu très sec » ; he buys Odette's help with rubies to obtain leave « qu'il fît un voyage avec Morel ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage is organized as a sustained unmasking of Saint-Loup: the public figure of the impeccable husband and the world's version of his infidelities are peeled back by Jupien's and Aimé's disclosures to reveal a concealed second life, a feigned love for Rachel, and the purchase of his mother-in-law's complicity. The narrator endorses the exposure to the point of pain (« la vérité qui me fit une peine infinie »), so the local movement is a clear diminishment even though the world still sees only the good husband.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Un beau jour tout avait été changé, le gendre était devenu un ange » ; « Ainsi, grâce à Robert, pouvait-elle, au seuil de la cinquantaine (d'aucuns disaient de la soixantaine), éblouir chaque table où elle allait dîner […] d'un luxe inouï » ; « elle n'avait jamais été aussi élégante ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Odette's local social standing plainly rises — she reverses her denunciation of her son-in-law and ends the passage dazzling every table she visits, more elegant than ever — but the narrator ironizes the mechanism (the reversal is bought, the protector is a son-in-law who does not like women, the age parenthesis and the « chasteté finale » undercut her), so the elevation is real socially and deflating in appraisal.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup is clearly diminished here: his marriage is shown to rest on deception, his devotion to Rachel is called a comedy, he has become « très sec », and he trades jewels for his mother-in-law's procurement of his wife's consent.

Gilberte loses ground emotionally as the deceived party who does not even know what she is deceived about, is left to get home from parties as best she can, and imitates Rachel's ribbons and hairstyle out of jealousy for a rival who no longer matters.
Her local standing rises: financed by Robert, she dazzles every dinner and evening with unheard-of luxury and has never been so elegant.

The narrator's irony lowers her personally: her volte-face on the son-in-law she had been bitterly « flétrissant » is openly venal, and her new splendour is framed as the last shift of a woman who has always needed to be kept.

ambiguities: « le jeune marquis de Cambremer », who signs himself Léonor and is said to take after his grandmother, is the young Cambremer who married Mlle d'Oloron, not the reference sheet's marquis de Cambremer (Cancan); he is therefore recorded with the passage's surface form and left unresolved.

The narrator explicitly discredits Aimé's testimony about the earlier Balbec period (« ou le liftier avait menti, ou c'était Aimé qui mentait »), so part of the evidence against Saint-Loup is presented as doubtful; the diminishment is nonetheless carried by Jupien's independent and uncontested disclosure about Bobette/Morel.

Odette's closing movement can be read either as a genuine late-life triumph (« elle n'avait jamais été aussi élégante ») or as an ironic diminishment; the annotation commits to both being present, with social gain and personal deflation recorded separately.
